title: The grid search
text: Each line is one set of inputs, scored at five strengths of C. The dashed line is the linear model on this site. Too small a C (far left) squeezes the weights and hurts every recipe. Past C = 0.1 the lines go flat, and the recipe with both additions sits lowest.

title: Against other model types
text: The same cross-validation for every model. Shorter bars are better. The bar axis does not start at zero, so the gaps look bigger than they are: top to bottom is about 1%. The simple models win, and the flexible ones (boosting, neural network) fit noise.

title: What each input is worth
text: The model's weights, each for one typical step (one standard deviation) of that input. Orange pushes toward the under, blue toward the over. Points still needed dwarfs the rest. Its squared term is the curve: it takes back some of that push when the number needed is very large or very small.

title: ROC curve
text: Sweep the cutoff from strict to loose and track how many overs the model catches against how many false alarms it raises, on the test seasons across a spread of totals. The closer the curve hugs the top-left corner the better. Area under it (AUC) is 0.81; a coin flip is 0.50.

title: Can you trust the percentages?
text: Test games are grouped by the chance the model gave them. Dots on the dashed line mean 70% really did go over about 70% of the time. Each dot is about 357 game-and-total pairs from the test seasons.

title: What the cutoff changes
text: Calling 'over' at 50% is a choice. Raise the cutoff and the model calls over less often (gray falls) but those calls are right more often (blue rises), while its under calls get less reliable (orange falls). This is the cutoff slider on the Prediction tab, drawn across its whole range.
